Direct `js_repl` calls must send raw JavaScript tool input (optionally with first-line `// codex-js-repl: timeout_ms=15000`). Do not wrap code in JSON (for example `{"code":"..."}`), quotes, or markdown code fences. - Helpers: `codex.cwd`, `codex.homeDir`, `codex.tmpDir`, `codex.tool(name, args?)`, and `codex.emitImage(imageLike)`. - `codex.tool` executes a normal tool call and resolves to the raw tool output object. Use it for shell and non-shell tools alike. Nested tool outputs stay inside JavaScript unless you emit them explicitly. - `codex.emitImage(...)` adds one image to the outer `js_repl` function output each time you call it, so you can call it multiple times to emit multiple images. It accepts a data URL, a single `input_image` item, an object like `{ bytes, mimeType }`, or a raw tool response object with exactly one image and no text. It rejects mixed text-and-image content. - `codex.tool(...)` and `codex.emitImage(...)` keep stable helper identities across cells. Saved references and persisted objects can reuse them in later cells, but async callbacks that fire after a cell finishes still fail because no exec is active. - Request full-resolution image processing with `detail: "original"` only when the `view_image` tool schema includes a `detail` argument. - A local builder copilot for one power user on macOS.
- Inputs: files, notes, browser tasks, desktop state, and lightweight voice notes.

- Packaging: one CLI, one local server, one memory store, one dashboard.

- A single technical builder/operator working locally on macOS, using Obsidian and local models, who wants retrieval, automation, and continuity without cloud dependence.

- “One local command surface for your files, notes, browser, and desktop, with persistent memory and minimal overhead.”

Three options on the table: 1. **Terminal-first** — keep the CLI as primary surface. Fast, composable, zero build step. But high intent gap for non-command tasks. 2. **Generative canvas** — use something like Google Stitch SDK to generate UI on the fly from prompts. Flexible but adds latency and external dependency. 3. **Hybrid** — a minimal shell (terminal + state panels) with canvas zones that agents can populate dynamically. I lean toward option 3. The shell stays fast and local. Canvas zones let us render rich content when needed without rebuilding the whole UI. What's your take? And what stack would you reach for? <subagent_notification> {"agent_path":"019d3281-3c9a-73a3-bdb6-fab0e6482265","status":{"completed":"**Current Surface**

The existing ComfyUI integration is thin and operational, not generative.

- [comfyui.ts](/Users/ummi/hii/src/tools/comfyui.ts#L6) defines the runtime boundary: local app path, `COMFYUI_URL`, MCP server dir, PID/log files, health checks, and model listing. It currently supports only `start`, `stop`, `status`, `logs`, and `models`.
- [cli.ts](/Users/ummi/hii/src/cli.ts#L499) exposes that boundary as `hii comfyui start|stop|status|logs|models`. There is no `create`, `run`, `prompt`, or artifact-returning command yet.

Do not wrap code in JSON (for example `{"code":"..."}`), quotes, or markdown code fences. - Helpers: `codex.cwd`, `codex.homeDir`, `codex.tmpDir`, `codex.tool(name, args?)`, and `codex.emitImage(imageLike)`. - `codex.tool` executes a normal tool call and resolves to the raw tool output object. Use it for shell and non-shell tools alike. Nested tool outputs stay inside JavaScript unless you emit them explicitly. - `codex.emitImage(...)` adds one image to the outer `js_repl` function output each time you call it, so you can call it multiple times to emit multiple images. It accepts a data URL, a single `input_image` item, an object like `{ bytes, mimeType }`, or a raw tool response object with exactly one image and no text. It rejects mixed text-and-image content. - `codex.tool(...)` and `codex.emitImage(...)` keep stable helper identities across cells. Saved references and persisted objects can reuse them in later cells, but async callbacks that fire after a cell finishes still fail because no exec is active. - Request full-resolution image processing with `detail: "original"` only when the `view_image` tool schema includes a `detail` argument. The same availability applies to `codex.emitImage(...)`: if `view_image.detail` is present, you may al...

Use this path. 1. On the PC, enable the SSH server. Open PowerShell as Administrator and run: ```powershell Get-WindowsCapability -Online | Where-Object Name -like 'OpenSSH.Server*' Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name OpenSSH.Server~~~~0.0.1.0 Start-Service sshd Set-Service -Name sshd -StartupType Automatic Get-Service sshd ``` If `sshd` shows `Running`, the server is up. 2. Allow SSH through the Windows firewall. ```powershell New-NetFirewallRule -Name sshd -DisplayName "OpenSSH Server (sshd)" -Enabled True -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -Action Allow -LocalPort 22 ``` 3. Find the PC’s IP address. ```powershell ipconfig ``` Use the IPv4 address for the active adapter, something like `192.168.1.42`. 4. From your Mac, connect with: ```bash ssh your_windows_username@192.168.1.42 ``` If it’s your first time, type `yes` at the host-key prompt, then enter your Windows password. 5. If it fails, check the usual causes. - Wrong Windows username. Run `whoami` on the PC to confirm. - PC and Mac not on the same network. - `sshd` not running: `Get-Service sshd` - Firewall rule missing. - Port `22` blocked or changed. If you want key-based login instead of passwords, on your Mac run: ```bash ssh-keygen -t ed25519 ssh-copy-id your_windows_username@192.168.1.42 ``` If `ssh-copy-id` isn’t installed on your Mac, I can give you the manual Windows key setup. If you want, I can also walk you through this interactively for your exact PC username and IP.

SSH is a secure way to control another computer from the terminal over a network. It gives you a remote shell, lets you run commands, move files, edit configs, and script admin work without sitting at the PC. You need it if you want things like: - remote terminal access to your PC from your Mac - file transfer with `scp` or `rsync` - running dev tools, servers, or scripts on the PC remotely - managing the machine headlessly You do not need it if your actual goal is: - seeing the desktop and clicking around - gaming remotely - using full GUI apps visually For those, Remote Desktop, Parsec, Sunshine/Moonlight, or AnyDesk usually make more sense. Rule of thumb: - Use `ssh` for command-line control. - Use remote desktop software for full-screen visual control. If your goal is “I want to access my PC from this Mac,” tell me whether you want terminal control or full desktop control, and I’ll point you to the right setup.

user_messages: Ummi, this is a strong open-source play. The winning product is not “AI inside Rhino.” The winning product is: **A local Rhino 8 + Grasshopper operating layer that lets Claude, Codex, Cursor, and ChatGPT control Rhino through MCP without buying AI modeling credits.** Think of it as: ```text Claude / Codex / Cursor / ChatGPT ↓ MCP Rhino MCP Server ↓ local bridge Rhino 8 + Grasshopper + Plugins ↓ Geometry, definitions, fabrication files, analysis, renders, documentation ``` McNeel already exposes the right developer surface: RhinoCommon is the core .NET API, Grasshopper has an SDK for custom components/data types, and Rhino 8 includes Python 3 via the ScriptEditor plus IronPython 2.7 support. ([www.rhino3d.com][1]) Rhino 8 also added key modeling capabilities worth exposing directly, including ShrinkWrap, SubD Creases, PushPull workflows, better drafting tools, faster rendering, and new Grasshopper data types. ([www.rhino3d.com][2]) ## 1. The product thesis Most AI Rhino tools are credit-based because they hide the model, cloud execution, or generation pipeline. Your server should do the opposite: ```text Own your model. Own your geometry. Own your files. Use your own Claude / Codex / ChatGPT / local LLM.
